ety.text: From Middle English suffisen, from Middle French souffire, from Latin sufficiō (“supply, be adequate”), from sub (“under”) + faciō (“do, make”). Cognate with French suffire.

senses.d: To be enough or sufficient; to meet the need (of anything); to be adequate; to be good enough.
ex: For this plum cake, two eggs should suffice.
To recount almighty works, / What words or tongue of seraph can suffice?

senses.d: To satisfy; to content; to be equal to the wants or demands of.
ex: A joint of lamb sufficed even his enormous appetite.
Lord Brougham's salary would have sufficed more than ninety Prussian judges.
During the festival, the temple suffices food to the beggars.
The king sufficed his army with food and weapons before the great battle.

Compare Sicilian bastari, Spanish and Portuguese bastar, French baster.

ety.text: From Old French sufisanz, soficient, from Latin sufficiēns, present participle of sufficiō.

ex: We have sufficient supplies to last the winter.
There is not sufficient access to the Internet in many small rural villages.

senses.d: A quantity (of something) that is as large as is needed.
ex: We don't need any more; we already have sufficient.
Sufficient of us are against this idea that we should stop now.

senses.d: Of a type or kind that suffices, that satisfies requirements or needs.
ex: This is a necessary condition but not a sufficient one.

senses.d: Possessing adequate talents or accomplishments; of competent power or ability; qualified; fit.
ex: They felt sufficient to maintain their present prosperity and independence.
I have never yet felt adequate. I have never yet felt sufficient.

senses.d: Having enough money to meet obligations and live comfortably.
